problems.title: The reciprocal lower bound can exceed one
problems.source_location: Theorem 3.1, Eq.(5), PDF pp.4–5; Appendix A.1, PDF pp.24–25, Eqs.(19)–(31)
claim: Theorem 3.1 claims \(P(\hat y_2\mid c)>\delta/(D_{\rm seq}+\epsilon)\) under its coherence and semantic-class assumptions.
analysis: Let one-token context \(c\) have probability \(1\), followed by completed responses \(a,b,r\) with probabilities \((0.4,0.4,0.2)\), then certain termination. Put \(a,b\) in the same semantic class, \(\tau=2\), \(\epsilon=0.01\). Coherence is \(\sqrt{2.5}<2\); the appendix gives \(\delta=1/4\), while \(D_{\rm seq}=\log(0.4/0.4)=0\). The theorem demands \(0.4>25\), despite meeting its small-argument condition. Linearizing an exponential and then dropping the added constant does not preserve a numerical lower bound.
result: The central reciprocal theorem is false under its own assumptions. No model or operational attack is needed.
assumptions: The model is a fully normalized terminating autoregressive law and the semantic map assigns the two abstract responses to one class.
repair: Retain the exact log-ratio identity \(P(\hat y_2\mid c)=P(\hat y_1\mid c)e^{-D_{\rm seq}}\), which gives lower bound \(\delta e^{-D_{\rm seq}}\). It does not prove semantic convergence by itself.
problems.impact_rationale: This is a glaring impossible-probability conclusion in a main theorem.
problems.existing_correction_status: An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: An improved representative can reduce semantic-class mass
problems.source_location: Theorem 3.2, Eq.(6), PDF p.6; Appendix A.2, PDF pp.26–27
claim: Theorem 3.2’s argument treats maximizing one representative as maximizing the class mass, without a stated approximation factor or fixed within-class proportions.
analysis: Two feasible contexts give class probabilities \((0.400,0.380)\) and \((0.395,0.395)\) for responses \(a,b\). Maximizing \(a\) selects the first, but class masses are \(0.780<0.790\). Embed the contexts with probabilities \(0.005\) each, certain response termination, \(\tau=100\) and \(\epsilon=0.01\); then \(\delta=0.0002\), all class probabilities are coherent and all ordered-pair small-ratio conditions hold. The monotonic implication fails independently of the first theorem.
result: Optimizer equivalence and the proof’s monotonicity are unsupported. An unspecified empirical approximation tolerance is not quantitatively refuted.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.
repair: Fixed positive proportions \(P(y_i\mid c)=w_iP(Y_\Phi\mid c)\), with \(w_i\) independent of context, are a sufficient condition for exact equivalence. They are not established properties of the models.
problems.impact_rationale: This limits an unquantified approximation interpretation; a numerical approximation-quality theorem was not supplied.
problems.existing_correction_status: An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: An infinite completed-response class cannot share a positive floor
problems.source_location: Definition 3.1, Eq.(2), PDF p.3; sequence domain in Section 3.1
claim: Definition 3.1 requires \(P(y_i\mid c)>\delta>0\) for every member of a potentially infinite semantic class.
analysis: Distinct completed responses are disjoint events. For any \(N\) members, normalization gives \(1\geq\sum_iP(y_i\mid c)>N\delta\), impossible once \(N>1/\delta\). A finite class requires \(N\delta<1\). Overlapping prefixes cannot instead be summed as completed-response mass.
result: The formulation needs a finite feasible domain or a different coverage objective. The implemented finite search is not shown empty.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.
repair: Specify a finite candidate class with compatible thresholds, or use a class-mass constraint. These are different objectives and do not automatically preserve Theorem 3.2.
problems.impact_rationale: This is a domain/feasibility qualification rather than demonstrated failure of the finite practical search.
problems.existing_correction_status: An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: Nucleus mass does not enforce a fixed token-probability floor
problems.source_location: Theorem 3.3 and Algorithm 1; Appendix B.2, PDF pp.28–29; baselines/sra/utils.py, GenerationWorker selector
claim: Theorem 3.3 uses per-token probability above \(1/\tau\), while the released selector uses cumulative top-p mass and top-k truncation.
analysis: Probabilities \((0.90,0.04,0.03,0.03)\) at top-p level \(0.95\) select the first three tokens. At \(\tau=20\), two are below \(0.05\). A one-token context of perplexity \(19.9\) followed by the \(0.03\) token has perplexity \(\sqrt{19.9/0.03}>20\). The selector contains no fixed-floor check.
result: Nucleus selection alone does not preserve the same fixed-threshold guarantee. The original sufficient theorem remains valid.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.
repair: Enforce the fixed floor or check cumulative perplexity directly. An adaptive threshold needs an explicit update and final validation before claiming its changed guarantee.
problems.impact_rationale: This is a selector/guarantee scope mismatch, with no measured practical attack-performance effect.
problems.existing_correction_status: An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.
